decks.title: Chemical Equations and Relative Masses — Part 1: Writing and balancing equations
goals: Write word and formula equations for reactions with one or two reactants and one or more products
State the information a balanced chemical equation conveys
Balance simple equations by the hit-and-trial method

slides.heading: A sentence in the language of chemistry
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a chemical equation tells the story of a reaction in a few symbols, and a balanced equation tells it truthfully.

visual.alt: Flow: reactants, reaction, products

slides.narration: When magnesium burns, a bright flame appears and a white powder is left. A chemical equation records exactly what went in and what came out. In this part we learn to write equations and to balance them.

slides.heading: Word equation and formula equation
slides.body_md: A **chemical equation** is a shorthand way of showing a chemical change using symbols and formulae. The substances before the arrow are **reactants**; those after it are **products**.

visual.alt: Table showing the word equation, skeletal equation and balanced equation for magnesium burning

slides.narration: A word equation uses names. A formula equation replaces them with symbols and formulae. The first formula equation we write is skeletal, because it is not yet balanced. The final balanced version has numbers in front of some formulae.

slides.heading: One reactant, several products
slides.body_md: Heating **ammonium dichromate**: one reactant breaks into **three** products. The orange crystals swell up and leave a fluffy green powder.

visual.alt: Ammonium dichromate on heating gives nitrogen, chromium(III) oxide and water
visual.caption: One reactant, three products.

slides.narration: Some reactions have only one reactant. When ammonium dichromate is heated, it breaks down into nitrogen gas, green chromium oxide and steam. The triangle above the arrow stands for heat.

slides.heading: Two reactants, one product
slides.body_md: Magnesium and oxygen **combine**. Two reactants form a **single** product, magnesium oxide.

visual.alt: Two magnesium plus one oxygen gives two magnesium oxide
visual.caption: Two reactants, one product.

slides.narration: In this reaction two substances join to make one. Two atoms of magnesium combine with one molecule of oxygen to give two units of magnesium oxide.

slides.heading: Two reactants, several products
slides.body_md: Copper reacts with **concentrated nitric acid** to give **three** products: copper nitrate, a brown gas and water.

visual.alt: Copper plus four nitric acid gives copper nitrate, two nitrogen dioxide and two water
visual.caption: Two reactants, three products.

slides.narration: Many reactions have more than one product. Copper and concentrated nitric acid give copper nitrate, a brown gas called nitrogen dioxide, and water.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a reaction
slides.body_md: Copper reacts with concentrated nitric acid to give copper nitrate, nitrogen dioxide and water.

visual.alt: Reactants and products of the copper and nitric acid reaction

slides.narration: How many reactants and how many products does this reaction have?

slides.heading: What a balanced equation tells us
slides.body_md: Take the balanced equation $\ce{2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO}$.

rows: Magnesium and oxygen react; magnesium oxide forms
2 atoms of Mg + 1 molecule of O₂ → 2 units of MgO
Heat, written above the arrow, and (s), (l), (g), (aq) if needed

visual.alt: Table of the information given by the equation for magnesium burning

slides.narration: A balanced equation names the substances, shows how many atoms or molecules of each take part, and gives their relative masses. Forty eight parts of magnesium and thirty two parts of oxygen make eighty parts of magnesium oxide. Nothing is lost.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading an equation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2}$ find the total relative mass of the reactants and of the products. (Zn = 65, H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)

**Step 1.** Reactants: $65 + 98 = 163$.

**Step 2.** Products: $161 + 2 = 163$.

**Step 3.** The totals are equal: mass is conserved.

visual.alt: Table of the relative masses of the four substances in the zinc and sulphuric acid reaction

slides.narration: Add the relative masses on each side. Zinc is sixty five and sulphuric acid is ninety eight, so the reactants total one hundred and sixty three. Zinc sulphate is one hundred and sixty one and hydrogen is two, so the products also total one hundred and sixty three. The two sides agree.

slides.heading: Quick check: what the equation says
slides.body_md: Look at the numbers in front of each formula.

visual.alt: Two magnesium plus one oxygen gives two magnesium oxide

slides.narration: Which statement about this equation is correct?

slides.heading: Balancing by hit and trial

nodes.label: Write the correct formulae of reactants and products
Count the atoms of each element on both sides
Put a number in front of a formula to change the count
Balance the element in the most complex formula first

visual.alt: Five steps for balancing an equation by hit and trial

slides.narration: Balancing is a careful game of trial and error. Write the right formulae first. Count the atoms on each side. Then change only the numbers in front of formulae, never the small numbers inside them. Recount at the end.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: balance aluminium burning in oxygen
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Balance $\ce{Al + O2 -> Al2O3}$.

**Step 1.** Oxygen: 2 on the left, 3 on the right. The least common multiple is 6, so use $3\ce{O2}$ and $2\ce{Al2O3}$.

**Step 2.** Aluminium on the right is now $2 \times 2 = 4$, so use $4\ce{Al}$.

**Step 3.** Check: Al 4 and 4; O 6 and 6.

visual.alt: Table checking the atoms of aluminium and oxygen on both sides of the balanced equation

slides.narration: Oxygen is the awkward one, two on the left and three on the right. Make both six, using three oxygen molecules and two aluminium oxide units. That gives four aluminium atoms on the right, so we need four on the left. Both sides now have four aluminium and six oxygen.

slides.heading: Balancing with groups of atoms
slides.body_md: Treat a radical such as hydroxide or phosphate as **one unit** if it appears unchanged on both sides. Balance $\ce{Ca(OH)2 + H3PO4 -> Ca3(PO4)2 + H2O}$.

visual.alt: Three calcium hydroxide plus two phosphoric acid gives calcium phosphate and six water
visual.caption: Ca 3 and 3; phosphate 2 and 2; H 12 and 12; O 14 and 14.

slides.narration: Keep the phosphate group together. Calcium needs three, so use three calcium hydroxide. Phosphate needs two, so use two phosphoric acid. Hydrogen and oxygen then fix the number of water molecules, which is six.

slides.heading: Quick check: balancing
slides.body_md: Balance magnesium burning in nitrogen.

visual.alt: Three magnesium plus one nitrogen gives magnesium nitride

slides.narration: Magnesium reacts with nitrogen to form magnesium nitride. Which set of numbers balances the equation?

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: A chemical equation shows reactants and products in symbols.
A balanced equation shows the substances, the number of particles, the relative masses, and the conditions and states.
Balance by changing the number in front of a formula, never a subscript.
Treat an unchanged radical as one unit when balancing.

visual.alt: Summary table of three kinds of equation

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. An equation lists reactants and products. A balanced one has the same atoms on both sides and shows the relative masses. Balance by hit and trial with numbers in front of formulae, and never alter a subscript.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write correct formulae before you balance.
Never change a subscript to balance; change the number in front.
Show a check of the atom count for each element.
Write state symbols and the heat sign if the question gives them.

rows: Recount every element at the end
Giving a balanced equation with no arrow

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips. Get the formulae right first. Fix the numbers in front, never the small numbers. Show your atom count, because it earns marks. And write conditions such as heat above the arrow when the question gives them.

decks.title: Chemical Equations and Relative Masses — Part 2: Relative masses and percentage composition
goals: Define relative atomic mass and relative molecular mass and state the standard they use
Calculate the relative molecular mass of a compound, including one with water of crystallisation
Calculate the percentage by mass of each element in a compound and the percentage of water in a hydrate

slides.heading: Weighing atoms by comparison
slides.body_md: Part 2 — atoms are far too small to weigh one by one, so chemists compare their masses with a standard.

visual.alt: Flow: relative atomic mass, relative molecular mass, percentage composition

slides.narration: No balance can weigh a single atom. Instead we say how many times heavier an atom is than a standard atom. From these numbers we get molecular masses, and then the percentage of each element in a compound.

slides.heading: Relative atomic mass
slides.body_md: **Relative atomic mass** is the number of times one atom of an element is **heavier than one-twelfth of an atom of carbon-12**. It is a ratio and has no unit.

slides.narration: Take one carbon twelve atom and cut its mass into twelve equal parts. One part is our unit. A hydrogen atom weighs one unit, a carbon atom twelve, an oxygen atom sixteen, and an iron atom fifty six. Chlorine is thirty five and a half.

slides.heading: The standard for atomic masses

rows: One-twelfth of its mass taken as 1

visual.alt: Table of the hydrogen standard and the carbon-12 standard

slides.narration: Earlier, the hydrogen atom was the standard, with a mass of one. Today the standard is one twelfth of a carbon twelve atom. The two scales give almost the same numbers, because a hydrogen atom has a mass very close to one unit.

slides.heading: Relative molecular mass
slides.body_md: **Relative molecular mass** is the number of times one molecule is heavier than one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom. It equals the **sum of the relative atomic masses** of all the atoms in the formula.

visual.alt: Table of relative molecular masses of four compounds with working

slides.narration: To find a relative molecular mass, add the atomic masses of every atom in the formula. Water is two plus sixteen, eighteen. Carbon dioxide is forty four. Ammonia is seventeen and sulphuric acid is ninety eight.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: aluminium sulphate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the relative molecular mass of $\ce{Al2(SO4)3}$. (Al = 27, S = 32, O = 16)

**Step 1.** Count atoms: Al 2, S 3, O 12.

**Step 2.** Multiply: $2 \times 27 = 54$; $3 \times 32 = 96$; $12 \times 16 = 192$.

**Step 3.** Add: $54 + 96 + 192 = 342$.

visual.alt: Table working out the relative molecular mass of aluminium sulphate

slides.narration: First count the atoms inside the bracket carefully. The bracket multiplies each atom by three, so sulphur is three and oxygen is twelve. Two aluminium is fifty four. Three sulphur is ninety six. Twelve oxygen is one hundred and ninety two. The total is three hundred and forty two.

slides.body_md: Count the atoms inside the bracket first. (Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)

slides.narration: Some crystals carry water inside their structure. Heating them in a test tube drives the water off as steam, which condenses on the cool wall. In the formula, a dot separates the salt from the water, and the water counts in the molecular mass.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a hydrated salt
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the relative molecular mass of $\ce{ZnSO4.7H2O}$. (Zn = 65, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)

**Step 1.** Anhydrous part: $65 + 32 + 4 \times 16 = 161$.

**Step 2.** Water part: $7 \times (2 \times 1 + 16) = 7 \times 18 = 126$.

**Step 3.** Total $= 161 + 126 = 287$.

visual.alt: Table working out the relative molecular mass of zinc sulphate crystals

slides.narration: Split the formula at the dot. The salt part comes to one hundred and sixty one. Seven water molecules weigh seven times eighteen, one hundred and twenty six. Add them to get two hundred and eighty seven.

slides.heading: Percentage composition
slides.body_md: The **percentage composition** of a compound is the mass of each element in 100 parts of the compound.

rows: Find the relative molecular mass of the compound
Find the total mass of the element (atoms × atomic mass)
Divide step 2 by step 1 and multiply by 100
The percentages must add up to 100

visual.alt: Table of four steps for percentage composition

math: \text{percentage of an element} = \frac{\text{mass of the element in one formula}}{\text{relative molecular mass}} \times 100
slides.narration: Percentage composition tells us how much of each element is present in a hundred parts of a compound. Divide the mass of the element by the molecular mass of the compound, and multiply by one hundred. The percentages must add up to one hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: magnesium sulphate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the percentage of each element in $\ce{MgSO4}$. (Mg = 24, S = 32, O = 16)

**Step 1.** Relative molecular mass $= 24 + 32 + 64 = 120$.

**Step 2.** Mg: $\frac{24}{120} \times 100 = 20\%$; S: $\frac{32}{120} \times 100 = 26.7\%$; O: $\frac{64}{120} \times 100 = 53.3\%$.

**Step 3.** Check: $20 + 26.7 + 53.3 = 100$.

visual.alt: Table of the percentage composition of magnesium sulphate

slides.narration: The molecular mass of magnesium sulphate is one hundred and twenty. Magnesium is twenty four out of one hundred and twenty, which is exactly twenty percent. Sulphur is just over twenty six percent and oxygen just over fifty three percent. They add up to one hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: percentage of water of crystallisation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the percentage of water in $\ce{FeSO4.7H2O}$. (Fe = 56, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)

**Step 1.** Relative molecular mass $= 152 + 126 = 278$.

**Step 2.** Water $= 7 \times 18 = 126$.

**Step 3.** Percentage $= \frac{126}{278} \times 100 = 45.3\%$.

visual.alt: Table of the percentage of anhydrous salt and of water in iron(II) sulphate crystals

slides.narration: The total mass of the crystals is two hundred and seventy eight. The seven water molecules account for one hundred and twenty six of it. One hundred and twenty six over two hundred and seventy eight, times one hundred, is about forty five point three percent.

slides.heading: Finding the mass of an element in a sample
slides.body_md: Use the percentage or the ratio of masses. In 204 g of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃ (RMM 102), the aluminium is $\frac{54}{102} \times 204 = 108$ g.

visual.alt: Table finding the mass of aluminium and oxygen in 204 grams of aluminium oxide

slides.narration: Once you know a ratio, you can scale it. Fifty four parts out of one hundred and two of aluminium oxide are aluminium. In two hundred and four grams of the oxide that is one hundred and eight grams of aluminium, and ninety six grams of oxygen.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Relative atomic mass: how many times an atom is heavier than one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom; no unit.
Relative molecular mass: the sum of the relative atomic masses in the formula.

sections.heading: 1. Chemical equations
sections.body_md:
A **chemical equation** is a shorthand way of showing a chemical change using symbols and formulae. **Reactants** are written before the arrow and **products** after it.

| Kind of reaction | Word equation | Formula equation |
|---|---|---|
| One reactant, several products | Ammonium dichromate → nitrogen + chromium(III) oxide + water | $\ce{(NH4)2Cr2O7 ->[\Delta] N2 + Cr2O3 + 4H2O}$ |
| Two reactants, one product | Magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide | $\ce{2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO}$ |
| Two reactants, several products | Copper + nitric acid → copper nitrate + nitrogen dioxide + water | $\ce{Cu + 4HNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O}$ |

**A balanced equation tells us**
- the **substances** that react and form;
- the **number of atoms or molecules** of each (the numbers in front of the formulae);
- the **relative masses**: for 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 48 + 32 → 80, so total mass is the same on both sides;
- the **conditions** (such as heat, written above the arrow) and the **states** (s), (l), (g), (aq) when shown.

An equation does not tell how fast the reaction is, or whether it will happen in practice.

key_terms.definition_md: A shorthand representation of a chemical change using symbols and formulae.
Reactants are the substances that react; products are the substances formed.

sections.heading: 2. Balancing by hit and trial
sections.body_md:
The **law of conservation of mass** requires the same number of atoms of each element on both sides. To balance:

1. Write the correct formulae of all reactants and products.
2. Count atoms of each element on both sides.
3. Put a **number in front of a formula** to make the counts equal. Start with the element in the most complex formula, and leave hydrogen and oxygen for last.
4. **Never change a subscript**: that would change the substance.
5. Recount every element.

| Skeletal equation | Balanced equation |
|---|---|
| Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃ | 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ |
| Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂ | 3Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂ |
| Ca(OH)₂ + H₃PO₄ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + H₂O | 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2H₃PO₄ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 6H₂O |

A radical that stays unchanged on both sides (such as PO₄ or OH) can be balanced as one unit.

key_terms.definition_md: Balancing an equation by trying numbers in front of formulae until every element has the same count on both sides.

sections.heading: 3. Relative atomic mass and relative molecular mass
sections.body_md:
**Relative atomic mass** of an element is the number of times one atom of the element is heavier than **one-twelfth of an atom of carbon-12**. (Earlier the standard was the hydrogen atom, taken as 1; the two scales give nearly the same values.) It is a ratio, so it has no unit.

**Relative molecular mass** of a compound is the number of times one molecule of it is heavier than one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom. It is the **sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms** in the formula.

Atomic masses used: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, Al 27, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40, Fe 56, Cu 63.5, Zn 65.

| Compound | Working | RMM |
|---|---|---|
| H₂O | 2 × 1 + 16 | 18 |
| CO₂ | 12 + 2 × 16 | 44 |
| Ca(OH)₂ | 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) | 74 |
| Al₂(SO₄)₃ | 2 × 27 + 3 × 32 + 12 × 16 | 342 |
| ZnSO₄·7H₂O | 161 + 7 × 18 | 287 |

For a hydrate, add the **water of crystallisation** (the number of water molecules × 18). Some books write "relative molecular mass in u"; here it has no unit.

The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in one molecule (or formula unit).

sections.heading: 4. Percentage composition
sections.body_md:
The **percentage composition** of a compound gives the mass of each element in 100 parts by mass of the compound.

$$\text{percentage of an element} = \frac{\text{mass of the element in one formula}}{\text{relative molecular mass of the compound}} \times 100$$

**Magnesium sulphate, MgSO₄** (RMM 120): Mg 20%, S 26.7%, O 53.3%.

**Water of crystallisation.** Percentage of water in a hydrate = (mass of the water in one formula ÷ RMM of the hydrate) × 100. For FeSO₄·7H₂O: 126 ÷ 278 × 100 = 45.3%; for ZnSO₄·7H₂O it is 43.9%.

**Using a percentage.** A fixed fraction of a sample's mass is the element: in 204 g of Al₂O₃ the aluminium is 54 ÷ 102 × 204 = 108 g.

Percentages are rounded to one decimal place. The percentages of all the elements must add up to 100 (allow 99.9 or 100.1 from rounding).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Changing a subscript (writing MgO₂) to balance an equation instead of changing the number in front.
- Forgetting to multiply every atom inside a bracket by the number outside it.
- Leaving out the water of crystallisation when finding the relative molecular mass of a hydrate.
- Writing a unit such as g with a relative mass.
- Dividing by the mass of the element instead of the mass of the whole compound.
- Giving percentages that do not add up to 100.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a balanced equation, a relative molecular mass or one percentage.
- 2 marks: a calculation with the atomic masses stated and the working shown.
- 3 marks: working for percentage composition, with the final answer.
- 10-mark structured question: a situation or data with parts of 2 to 4 marks; show each step of every calculation and give units for masses.

questions.stem_md:
A student writes these skeletal equations in her notebook and has to balance them.

(i) H₂S + O₂ → SO₂ + H₂O

(ii) Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂

(iii) Al(OH)₃ + H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + H₂O

(a) Balance the three equations. [6]

(b) For equation (ii), state the ratio of molecules of carbon monoxide to molecules of carbon dioxide and the total relative mass of the reactants. (Fe = 56, C = 12, O = 16) [2]

(c) She tries to balance (iii) by changing Al(OH)₃ to Al₂(OH)₆. Explain why this is not allowed. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (i) $\ce{2H2S + 3O2 -> 2SO2 + 2H2O}$

(ii) $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$

(iii) $\ce{2Al(OH)3 + 3H2SO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + 6H2O}$

**(b)** CO : CO₂ = **3 : 3, that is 1 : 1**; total relative mass of reactants = 160 + 3 × 28 = **244**.

**(c)** Al₂(OH)₆ is **not the formula of aluminium hydroxide as the reactant is Al(OH)₃**; changing a subscript changes the substance, so only **the number in front** may be changed.

questions.solution_md: Three balanced equations; 1 : 1 and 244; subscripts fix the substance.

A student drops a few chips of marble (calcium carbonate) into dilute hydrochloric acid. The balanced equation is CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1, Cl = 35.5)

(a) Write the word equation for the reaction. [2]

(b) Calculate the total relative mass of the reactants and of the products to show that mass is conserved. [4]

(c) State two items of information, other than masses, that the equation gives. [2]

(d) State one observation and name the test for the gas formed. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide.**

**(b)** Reactants: 100 + 2 × 36.5 = **173**. Products: 111 + 18 + 44 = **173**. The totals are equal, so **mass is conserved**.

**(c)** The **substances** that react and form, and the **numbers of particles** (1 unit of calcium carbonate reacts with 2 molecules of hydrochloric acid).

**(d)** **Brisk effervescence** (bubbles of gas) is seen; the gas **turns lime water milky**.

questions.solution_md: Word equation; 173 on each side; substances and numbers of particles; fizzing and the lime water test.

questions.stem_md:
Magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, is used to make tofu and to control dust on roads. (Mg = 24, Cl = 35.5)

(a) Define relative atomic mass. [2]

(b) Calculate the relative molecular mass of magnesium chloride. [2]

(c) Calculate the percentage of chlorine in it, correct to one decimal place. [3]

(d) State how many times heavier one formula unit of MgCl₂ is than (i) one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom and (ii) a hydrogen atom, and say why the two answers are almost the same. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The number of times **one atom of the element is heavier than one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom**.

**(b)** 24 + 2 × 35.5 = 24 + 71 = **95**.

**(c)** Chlorine = 71 ÷ 95 × 100 = **74.7%**.

**(d)** (i) **95 times**; (ii) about **95 times** too (using H = 1). They agree because **a hydrogen atom has a mass of almost one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom**, that is about one unit.

questions.solution_md: Definition; 95; 74.7%; 95 and 95 since hydrogen is about one unit.

(a) Write the word equation. [1]

(b) Write the balanced formula equation, showing the heat sign. [2]

(c) State two observations from the experiment. [2]

(d) Say how many reactants and how many products there are. [1]

(e) Copy and complete the table to show that the atoms balance. [4]

| Element | Atoms on the left | Atoms on the right |
|---|---|---|
| N | | |
| H | | |
| Cr | | |
| O | | |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Ammonium dichromate → nitrogen + chromium(III) oxide + water (steam).**

**(b)** $\ce{(NH4)2Cr2O7 ->[\Delta] N2 + Cr2O3 + 4H2O}$

**(c)** The orange crystals **swell and glow with sparks**, and a **green powder** is left (nitrogen is given off).

**(d)** **One** reactant and **three** products.

**(e)** N 2 and 2; H 8 and 8; Cr 2 and 2; O 7 and 7.
